bio.en: Ryan J. Salva is VP of Product at GitHub, where he incubated and launched GitHub Copilot - one of the most transformative developer tools of the decade - and previously spent a decade at Microsoft and started in philosophy and English.
bio.zh: Ryan J. Salva 是 GitHub 的产品副总裁，在 GitHub 他孵化并推出了 GitHub Copilot——十年来最具变革性的开发者工具之一——此前他在微软工作十年，学术背景始于哲学与英语。

summary.en: Ryan tells the story of how GitHub Copilot went from a small R&D bet to a product used by millions, and what it takes to incubate a big bet inside a large company. He shares how Copilot keeps developers in flow by bringing context into the editor, and surprising use cases - from educators teaching kids to code to small businesses building internal tools with student teams. The episode is a fascinating look at building AI developer tooling at scale.
summary.zh: Ryan 讲述了 GitHub Copilot 如何从一个小小的研发赌注，成长为被数百万人使用的产品，以及在大公司内部孵化大型赌注需要什么。他分享了 Copilot 如何通过把上下文带进编辑器，让开发者保持在“心流”中，以及一些出人意料的使用场景——从教育者教孩童写代码，到小企业与学徒团队共建内部工具。本期是对规模化打造 AI 开发者工具的精彩透视。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: We had actually created a snapshot of GitHub's public code for what we call the Arctic Code Vault, right? Essentially, this is up in like way in the Northlands of Finland, there's a seed vault. We were like, you know what? Seed vaults are really there to preserve the diversity of the world's flora in seeds in case of some crazy either natural or manmade disaster. But another really important asset to the world is our code, our open source. This represents actually a lot of the collective, well, certainly software, if not intelligence of kind of the modern world, right?
turns.zh: 实际上，我们为GitHub的公共代码创建了一个快照，称之为"北极代码库"。基本上，它位于芬兰北部，那里有一个种子库。我们当时就想，种子库的存在是为了在发生自然或人为灾害时，保护全球植物种子的多样性。但对世界来说，另一个至关重要的资产就是我们的代码、我们的开源软件。这实际上代表了现代世界的大量集体智慧，如果不是全部的话。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: We had put this snapshot of public repositories on this silver film that would be preserved for thousands of years in this Arctic Code Vault. Well, we took that same data snapshot and we brought it to our friends over at OpenAI to see like, okay, what can we do with these large language models built on public code? Well, it turns out we can do some pretty cool things.
turns.zh: 我们将这个公共仓库的快照存储在银质薄膜中，以便在北极代码库中保存数千年。然后，我们将同样的数据快照带给OpenAI的团队，探讨如何利用基于公共代码构建的大型语言模型做些有趣的事情。结果发现，我们能做一些相当酷的事情。

turns.en: I'm excited as well. turns.zh: 我也很激动。我们在录制前简短交流过，你提到了自己的背景。对于在GitHub担任产品负责人的人来说，这段经历相当独特。能否分享一下你的求学经历，以及它如何引导你走上产品管理之路？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Oh wow! You're going to make me remember all the way back to school. Okay. Back in school, I was not a classic software engineering, CS major. The kind of esoteric answer is philosophy of aesthetics and 20th century critical theory. The easier access answer is philosophy and English. But primarily it was really about how do we, as people, communicate with each other, how do we express ourselves through creativity. As humans since the dawn of time have been painting on cave walls and dancing around the fire and writing stories and novels and singing to each other. I was just really interested in how we convey our experience of the world to others.
turns.zh: 哇哦！你要让我把记忆拉回学生时代了。好吧。我在大学时并非典型的软件工程或计算机科学专业。说个深奥点的，我的专业是20世纪批判理论和美学哲学。说个浅显点的，是哲学和英语。但最根本的是，我一直关注人类如何通过创造力相互交流、表达自我。自古以来，人类就在洞壁上作画、围着篝火跳舞、创作故事和小说，试图传递对世界的感知。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: I got started in software development and product management because I wanted to be in the business of creativity. We're at a really, really unique time in human history where we actually get to witness the advent of a brand new medium. Software development and the worlds that it creates wasn't possible, I don't know, maybe 50, 60 years ago now. If I'd been born in the 1700s, I probably would've been the guy making, I don't know, new colors of paint and paint brushes, but I wasn't. I was born kind of at the turn of the 21st century, and so I work in engineering.
turns.zh: 我之所以投身软件开发和产品管理，是因为我想参与创造性事业的浪潮。我们正处在人类历史上一个独特的时代，见证着一种全新媒介的诞生。50、60年前，要是生在18世纪，我可能还在调制新颜料、制作画笔，但我生于21世纪之交，所以选择了工程领域。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: That's what I've been doing for the last about a little bit more than 20 years now, working sometimes in startups, some of them other people, some of them my own, about 10 years at Microsoft and now three years at GitHub.
turns.zh: 过去二十多年来，我一直致力于此——有时在初创公司工作，有时自主创业，在微软待了10年，如今在GitHub已有三年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I didn't know that was a job to make new paint colors for paint brushes. Is there a color you would come up with?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我之前都不知道给画笔调配新颜色也是一份工作。你会想出什么颜色呢？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Oh man! It so happens that yellow... I think I would do a really vibrant gold sunshine yellow if I was in that business.
turns.zh: 天哪！说到黄色……如果我做这行，我会调配一种非常鲜艳的金色日光黄。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very positive, happy. I love it. That could be a new GitHub brand color. Today, you're VP of product at GitHub. Before that, you were a super senior product leader at Microsoft, and I'm always curious how that transition happens when you move from just a longtime senior product leader at a larger company to taking on something like this that was an acquisition. I'm curious what made you decide to take this leap, and then just was there anything interesting about the machination that went into just making that transition and figuring that out?
turns.zh: 非常积极、欢快。我喜欢这个主意。这或许可以成为GitHub的新品牌色。如今你是GitHub的产品副总裁。在此之前，你在微软担任过高级产品负责人，转到被收购的GitHub时经历了怎样的转变？是什么促使你做出这个决定？整个过渡过程中有没有什么有趣的幕后故事？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Yeah, it's a good question. Like I said, I was working on development tools and developer services when I was there at Microsoft. Specifically, I was leading product for what they call One Engineering System. It's essentially the shared developer infrastructure for all Microsoft products like Windows and Office and Azure and things like that, as well as Microsoft's DevOps solution called Azure DevOps. When the acquisition happened, it was clear that so much of the energy, so much of the focus and the innovation that was going to be happening around developer tools and services was going to be happening around GitHub. I mean, that's where the community is creating.
turns.zh: 是的，这是个好问题。正如我之前所说，我在微软时专注于开发工具和开发者服务，特别是领导One Engineering System的产品线。这套系统为Windows、Office、Azure等微软产品，以及微软的DevOps解决方案Azure DevOps提供共享的开发者基础设施。收购发生后，很明显，围绕开发者工具和服务的大部分精力、关注点和创新都将聚焦于GitHub。这里才是开发者社区的活力所在。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: That's where people are learning, that's where so much of the mind share of just the development community is focused. Like I said, I'm motivated. What I care about is helping people create. It was very clear to me that there was no place that I could have a larger impact than working at GitHub. I really took that opportunity to make the transition out of a little bit more enterprise focused internal role at Microsoft to going where I could work on everything from, I don't know, AI technology like Copilot to a cloud hosted development environments like Codespaces, repos, which literally every single developer on the planet is participating in some way GitHub repos in a typical year.
turns.zh: 这里是人们学习的场所，也是开发者社区思想交流的核心阵地。正如我所说，我热衷于帮助人们创造价值。我很清楚，在GitHub能产生更大的影响力远超在微软的企业级内部角色。因此，我抓住机会从微软转向GitHub，从专注于内部产品的角色转向开发者生态的全方位探索——从Copilot这样的AI技术，到Codespaces这样的云托管开发环境，再到GitHub仓库，这些仓库在典型一年里几乎涵盖了全球每位开发者的开发活动。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: That was what I wanted to accomplish, is just like, how do I get more connected to the community, especially the community outside of what Microsoft could reach on its own. The decision to move as well, I think, was really focused not just on what GitHub was and maybe is at the time, but what GitHub also can be. I mean, GitHub has more than a decade, nearly a decade and a half of history of bringing developers together to collaborate on code through repositories. But in the last few years, we've really expanded that portfolio to include so many different parts of the developer life cycle.
turns.zh: 我的目标是如何更好地融入社区，尤其是微软自身无法触及的社区。做出转换的决定不仅关乎GitHub当时的现状，更着眼于它未来的潜力。GitHub拥有十多年、近十五年的历史，通过仓库将开发者聚集在一起进行代码协作。但近年来，我们已将产品组合扩展至开发者生命周期的多个维度。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Again, I talked there about Codespaces and Copilot, but it's also actions for CI/CD and advanced security. As developers, we are so much more than just where we put our code. There's a whole part of the tool chain there. And to get to an opportunity to work on so many V1 products, like that is creation itself, to be able to build an entirely new product, get it out to market, test it, iterate on it, and really feed on the energy that's coming back from the community.
turns.zh: 我之前提到了Codespaces和Copilot，但还有CI/CD和高级安全等功能。作为开发者，我们远不止于代码存储的平台。整个工具链中还有诸多环节。能参与众多初代产品的开发，比如构建全新产品、推向市场、测试迭代，再从社区反馈中汲取养分，这本身就是创造的乐趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. There's definitely a lot of energy coming out of GitHub. What I want to spend most of our time chatting about is a product that your team helped launch and incubate, which is GitHub Copilot, which just from my outsider perspective feels like one of the biggest advances in software development in, I don't know, a decade, maybe more. It's definitely one of the most magical products out there and your team and you kind of led the incubation and launch of the Copilot.
turns.zh: 太棒了。GitHub 确实释放了巨大的创新活力。今天我想重点聊聊你们团队助力孵化和推出的产品——GitHub Copilot。单从外行视角看，它堪称过去十年乃至更长时间里软件开发领域最重大的进步之一。这绝对是市面上最具魔力的产品之一，而你们团队在Copilot的孵化和推出过程中发挥了关键作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love to spend most of our time chatting through that. The first question... Okay, cool. My first question just for folks that don't know a lot about Copilot is just like, what is it? Can you just kind of briefly describe what Copilot is?
turns.zh: 接下来，我想重点探讨这个产品。首先，对于不熟悉Copilot的朋友，我先简单介绍一下：Copilot是什么？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Yeah, sure. Developers for the last 20 years or more have had essentially simple, intelligent autocomplete. You hit the period and you get the next variable that might come up. It's helpful for moving a little bit faster through your code, helpful sometimes for remembering what the particular syntax might look like for a method or a function. Copilot is essentially that magnified by many lines of code. It is multi-line autocomplete that is fundamentally powered by an AI model called CodeX, which is a derivative of another one that you might be familiar with, GPT-3.
turns.zh: 好的，我来解释一下。过去20多年来，开发者主要使用的是简单但智能的代码补全功能——比如输入句点后自动补全可能出现的变量。这有助于提高编码效率，有时还能帮助记忆某个方法或函数的语法。Copilot则将这种功能扩展到多行代码层面。它基于名为CodeX的人工智能模型（该模型源自GPT-3），为编辑器（如VS Code、IntelliJ等）提供多行代码补全服务。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: When you are in the editor, it could be VS Code, it could be IntelliJ, it could be them, essentially, as you are typing, Copilot will provide suggestions usually in kind of this italicized gray text that is really, to your point, kind of magical what it's able to infer. Based upon the variables around it, the class names, the method names around it, your comments, Copilot infers what you intend to create, and then hopefully does a pretty good job at nailing it by providing scaffolding code template that you can then riff on. Now, what we tend to find is that developers love it. They really enjoy it. They kind of find themselves getting a little addicted to it because it helps them stay in the flow.
turns.zh: 当你使用编辑器时，Copilot会实时提供建议，通常以斜体灰色文本呈现。正如你所说，它能智能推断代码上下文，根据变量、类名、方法名、注释等，准确预测你的编码意图，并通过提供模板代码帮助你快速完成开发。开发者对此赞不绝口，因为它能让他们保持专注，提升工作效率。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: As developers, we love to be in that place. I love to be in that place where I'm creating things, where I'm focusing on some product, some piece of software that I'm going to give to my customers, my users. The labor of remembering what's the order of parameters that need to come into a particular API, or hey, what's the particular syntax of this thing I'm supposed to do, or oh, I've got to create a bunch of dummy data that is days of the week or months in the year. That's just labor. It's not creating. It's just typing.
turns.zh: 作为开发者，我们都渴望沉浸在创造的状态中。我们喜欢专注于产品开发，致力于为用户打造优质软件。例如，查找API参数顺序、解析语法结构、创建虚假数据等，这些重复性工作实在令人厌烦。Copilot通过将所有信息整合到编辑器中，省去了查阅文档、观看教程或在 Stack Overflow 上提问的繁琐步骤，让开发者能专心致志地编写代码。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Copilot helps developers stay in the flow by bringing all of that information into the editor, preventing them from having to go check out documentation or watch tutorial or go to Stack Overflow and either find an answer or worse, have to ask a question and wait for an answer. It just brings all of that into the editor and gives the developer often multiple suggestions that they can choose from and just pick and choose what is the right solution to solve the problem for the thing they're trying to create.
turns.zh: Copilot的魔力在于，它能将所有信息整合到编辑器中，让开发者无需手动查找文档、观看教程或在 Stack Overflow 上提问。它会根据上下文提供多个建议，帮助开发者快速找到正确的解决方案，专注于核心任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. What I'm most curious about, and we're going to spend time on this, is just how a product like this comes to be at a larger company. But before we get into that, what's the craziest story of someone using Copilot to write code? And I'll share one real quick. I was watching some YouTube videos to prepare for this chat and one guy, maybe this is the Turing Test of AI writing code, is he used Copilot to center divs. He's like, "Wow! This did it right." And then another guy, he's an instructor of code.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我最感兴趣的是——我们稍后会详细探讨这个问题——像Copilot这样的产品是如何在大型公司中诞生的。但在深入探讨之前，有没有人用Copilot写代码的最离奇故事？我先快速分享一个。为准备这次对话，我看了一些YouTube视频，其中有个用户用Copilot来居中div元素。他惊呼：“哇！这写得太准确了！” 还有个用户，是位编程指导老师。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He makes YouTube videos teaching people how to code and he's like, "Copilot just gives you the answer immediately, and so I can't make these videos as easily. I have to turn it off so that doesn't just give it away." I'm curious, what have you seen?
turns.zh: 他在YouTube上制作教人们如何编程的视频，他说：“Copilot会直接给出答案，这样我就不太容易制作这些视频了。我得把它关掉，免得答案被轻易泄露。” 我很好奇，你都见过哪些情况呢？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: There are so many of those. I'll just kind of give a couple of recent ones that I've heard. I was talking to one developer who was... He's actually an educator and he's teaching kids how to code, usually like kind of high school age, so 16, 15, that kind of thing. His experience matches my own, which is that many of us, we learn to code best not by arbitrary exercises, but by actually building something that's going to be useful solving problems.
turns.zh: 这种情况实在太多了。我只想举几个最近听说过的例子。我曾和一位开发者交流过——他实际上是一名教育工作者，专门教孩子们编程，学生年龄通常在16岁、15岁左右。他的经历和我不谋而合，那就是我们大多数人学习编程的最佳方式，不是通过随意的练习，而是通过实际开发对解决问题有用的工具。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: What he does is he matches small businesses and medium size businesses who need to build internal tools with essentially classes of students, like a group of maybe six or eight students, and then gives those students Copilot and says, "Here, small business, medium size business. Group of students, go build this internal tool for this business."
turns.zh: 他的做法是，将需要开发内部工具的中小型企业与学生班级（通常由六到八名学生组成）进行配对，然后给这些学生提供Copilot，并对中小型企业说：“现在，学生们为这家企业开发一个内部工具吧。”

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Copilot is essentially kind of whispering in the student's ear, metaphorically speaking, "Hey, here's how you solve this problem. Here's how you do this," and students build not only the tool, the software that the business needs and then get to put that on their resume and their application for college and university, but they also get to learn by using the tools that likely are going to be part of the core DNA of the developer tool chain two, three, four years from now, as AI starts to permeate our entire stack. That was a pretty cool recent one that I talked to.
turns.zh: 用通俗的话来说，Copilot就像是在学生耳边低语：“嘿，问题是这样解决的。步骤是这样的。” 学生们不仅能开发出企业所需的工具和软件，写入简历并用于大学申请，还能通过使用这些工具来学习。这些工具很可能在未来两三年内成为开发者工具链的核心组成部分，因为人工智能正在渗透到我们的整个技术栈中。我最近和一些人交流过，他们对此都赞不绝口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is very cool. I didn't think about just the education lever here of just making it so much easier to learn to code, not even just building code.
turns.zh: 这真是太棒了。我之前没想到它不仅能让学习编程变得容易得多，甚至连代码的编写过程都能优化。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: And that's the thing, Copilot is particularly good not just at taking away some of the effort, but often... There's learning a new language, and then there's also just waiting into a code base that you're not necessarily familiar with, right? I mean, heck, sometimes I don't recognize some of the code that I wrote six months ago or a year ago. It feels like I'm wading into new territory. But maybe you need to fix a bug in an app that you don't often touch, wading into that code base is kind of learning and creating a mental map for that code base.
turns.zh: 关键在于，Copilot不仅能减轻开发者的负担，还能……比如学习一门新语言，或者面对一个自己不熟悉的代码库。说真的，我有时连自己半年前或一年前写的代码都认不出来了，感觉就像要重新探索未知领域。但也许你需要修复一个不常接触的应用中的bug，面对这个代码库时，就是在学习并构建这个代码库的思维导图。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: One of the really magical pieces of Copilot here is that, that AI is collecting context of the application that you're going into. It can help you build that mental map and learn the code base, even if it's a language that you're already familiar with.
turns.zh: Copilot最神奇的地方在于，它能收集你正在处理的应用的上下文信息。即使是熟悉的语言，它也能帮助你构建思维导图，快速掌握代码库。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Going back to the beginning of Copilot and how it started, I'm always curious how a project that ends up being a huge deal to a larger company begins and especially how it builds momentum, how it gets buy in, and then just gets out the door. Can you talk about just the original seed of this idea like, who did it come from, who had the original vision, how did this idea emerge and build momentum where you put resources into it?
turns.zh: 太棒了。回到Copilot的起源和发展历程，我一直很好奇一个最终对大公司产生重大影响的项目是如何起步的，尤其是它如何积聚势头、获得支持，最终得以推向市场。你能否谈谈这个创意最初的萌芽阶段，比如它来自谁，最初的愿景是谁，这个想法是如何形成并积聚势头，最终投入资源加以推进的？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Oh wow, what a long, and I don't know, depending upon your point of view, sorted or exciting story that is. Microsoft and OpenAI have been collaborating for quite a while now on large language models, making its way into all different experiments and different parts of both Microsoft's software portfolio, as well as just helping OpenAI by providing the compute necessary. It takes massive amounts of compute to train these models. They were mostly large language models. Couple years ago now, it kind of dawned on us that, well, language models aren't just English and Spanish and German and Korean and Japanese, but Python and JavaScript and Java and C# and Closure.
turns.zh: 哇，真是个漫长且——视角不同，可能令人惊叹或兴奋的故事。微软和OpenAI在大型语言模型方面合作已久，这些模型已应用于微软的各类实验和软件组合中，同时微软还通过提供必要的计算资源助力OpenAI。训练这些模型需要海量算力，而当时主要使用的是大型语言模型。两年前，我们突然意识到，语言模型不只是英语、西班牙语、德语、韩语和日语，还包括Python、JavaScript、Java、C#和Closure等语言。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: All of these are languages too. In fact, they're kind of nice from an AI perspective because they're relatively constrained in terms of their semantics, right? The number of words, I put that the in scare quotes as it were, that can be expressed in Python, for example, is much smaller than the English language, which has all sorts of different grammar rules and nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs. We started to see what it would be like to actually bring code to these large language models. The way that I actually got introduced to it is kind of funny. Microsoft and OpenAI had this idea.
turns.zh: 这些语言也都是编程语言。从AI角度看，它们语义限制较多，相对更易理解。例如，Python能表达的词汇量远小于英语，后者有各种语法规则和名词、动词、形容词、副词。我们开始探索如何将代码引入这些大型语言模型。我的接触过程还挺有趣的。微软和OpenAI当时有个想法。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: At the time, one of the teams that I was responsible for was GitHub's infrastructure team, the team responsible for our data centers, our reliability, our rep time. We noticed one day that we were getting hammered, I mean absolutely hammered with a tremendous amount of clone requests. We're like, "Oh my gosh! Is this like a denial of service attack? How are we going to respond to this? What's going to happen?" We figured out pretty quickly that it was actually OpenAI. They were cloning all of our repositories to harvest the data out of GItHub.I mean, it's totally legit practice, but it does have a real consequence.
turns.zh: 当时，我负责的团队之一是GitHub的基础设施团队，负责数据中心、可靠性和响应时间。我们发现有一天服务器被大量克隆请求压垮了。我们当时惊呼：“天哪！这是拒绝服务攻击吗？我们该如何应对？会出什么事？”很快我们发现其实是OpenAI在克隆我们的所有仓库以获取GitHub数据。这完全合法，但确实会带来实际影响。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: We were able to step in and mitigate it very quickly. There was not a reliability kind of an uptime incident there, but we're like, "Hey, you all, cool. Love this thing. Let's see if we can get that data to you in a more responsible way, in a way that's packaged a little bit more to meet your needs." What we did is just the year before that, We had actually created a snapshot of GitHub's public code for what we call the Arctic Code Vault, right? Essentially, this is up in like way in the Northlands of Finland, there's a seed vault. We were like, you know what? Seed vaults are really there to preserve the diversity of the world's flora in seeds in case of some crazy either natural or manmade disaster.
turns.zh: 我们迅速介入并缓解了问题。虽然没有出现可靠性方面的宕机，但我们觉得：“嘿，伙计们，真不错。我们喜欢这个项目。看看能否以更负责任的方式、更符合你们需求的打包形式提供数据。”前一年，我们为GitHub的公共代码创建了快照，称之为“北极代码库”。这个库位于芬兰北部，类似种子库。我们想，种子库本质上是为了在自然或人为灾害发生时保存世界植物的多样性。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: But another really important asset to the world is our code, our open source. This represents actually a lot of the collective, well, certainly software, if not intelligence of kind of the modern world, right? This represents actually a lot of the collective, well, certainly software, if not intelligence of kind of the modern world. We had put this snapshot of public repositories on this silver film that would be preserved for thousands of years in this Arctic Code Vault. Well, we took that same data snapshot and we brought it to our friends over at OpenAI to see like, okay, what can we do with these large language models built on public code?
turns.zh: 然而，世界另一项极其重要的资产是我们的代码、我们的开源软件。事实上，这代表了现代世界的大量集体智慧——尤其是软件领域的智慧。正是这些开源代码，让我们得以将公共代码库的快照存储在北极代码库中，供后人研究数千年。我们还将同样的数据快照带给OpenAI的团队，探讨如何利用基于公共代码构建的大型语言模型实现创新应用。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Well, it turns out we can do some pretty cool things. Just like a translation tool that goes from English to Spanish, Spanish to German, you can also go from English to Python or Python to C#. We're like, okay, this is cool. We can start to get not only translation, but a little bit of predicted text here as well. We're all I think fairly already familiar with predictive text already in our code editors as IntelliSense. But in, I don't know, you go to your favorite word processor and chances are that you've got some kind of predictive text happening there as well.
turns.zh: 结果发现，我们能实现许多令人惊叹的功能。就像能将英文翻译成西班牙语、西班牙语翻译成德语的翻译工具一样，我们还能将英文翻译成Python，或将Python翻译成C#。我们不禁感叹，这太酷了！我们不仅能实现翻译功能，还能获取文本预测建议。想必大家对代码编辑器中的预测文本功能已经很熟悉，比如IntelliSense。但即便是在你常用的文本编辑器中，很可能也提供了类似的预测文本功能。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: We started experimenting with different user experiences, right? Do we want it so that you, I don't know, right click and get a little side panel that comes up with a bunch of different options for things that you might want here. That was nice because it would give you hold functions, but it's out of the cursor, right? You had to really... Even if you weren't switching over to a different window, you still had to switch over to a different panel, which itself was a little bit distracting. We eventually came to this idea of inline autocomplete.
turns.zh: 我们开始尝试不同的用户体验。例如，用户希望通过右键单击弹出侧边栏，获取一系列可能的功能选项。这虽然不错，但会让光标移出当前位置。即便不切换到其他窗口，也得切换到侧边栏，而侧边栏本身会分散注意力。最终，我们提出了内联自动补全的理念。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: We were able to with the kind of partnership of some of our friends over on the Microsoft side of things, partner with our friends in Visual Studio Code, they're like, hey, there's not really an extensibility yet in your editor for this multi-line autocomplete, but we've got an idea for how this might work. Played around with the actual presentation of it. What should the key strokes be? What should the presentation layer be? The gray italicized tech seemed to be a good way of indicating that it was ephemeral, as it were. Pretty early on, we landed on this user experience that is Copilot as most developers experience it today. I want to say that was at least 16 months ago, 14, 16 months ago. Since then, we brought it to developers.
turns.zh: 得益于微软团队的合作，我们与Visual Studio Code团队展开合作。他们发现编辑器中尚无支持多行自动补全的扩展功能，但他们提出了一个可行的方案。我们反复优化了呈现效果：快捷键如何设计？界面层如何设计？灰色斜体提示符似乎能有效传达临时性的提示信息。经过数月打磨，我们最终确定了如今开发者熟悉的Copilot用户体验。记得那时候应该是16个月前，或者14个月前，具体记不清了。此后，我们将这项技术推向了广大开发者群体。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to double click on that, you're saying just less than a year and a half ago, this kind of really started as a project and now it's out to the world. Is that right?
turns.zh: 你刚说这项技术不到一年半前就开始研发，现在已经面向全球开放，对吧？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: That is exactly right. That's exactly right. It's about a year and a half ago.
turns.zh: 没错，差不多就是一年半前。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's insane. What was that period between OpenAI almost taking down GitHub to I guess that point?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。从OpenAI差点让GitHub崩溃，到现在这项技术面向全球，期间经历了怎样的过程？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: The period in between kind of OpenAI almost taking down GitHub and then us really arriving at the user experience, part of that was, frankly, a lot of really smart researchers at OpenAI experimenting and doing what only world class AI researchers can do. It was a lot of them experimenting, occasionally asking for updates to the data set, tossing back to us a model that we might play with and tinker around with. These models have literally thousands of parameters that you can pass to them. When you're really thinking about GPT-3 and CodeX and then the transition from that to something like Copilot, it was not just like the model...
turns.zh: 开放式人工智能（OpenAI）差点让GitHub崩溃，而后我们才真正实现了用户体验。说实话，这其中很大程度上得益于OpenAI众多极其聪明的研究人员不断进行实验和探索，他们做着只有世界级AI研究者才能做到的事情。他们反复试验，偶尔要求更新数据集，交给我们可以玩味和调整的模型。这些模型有成千上万个可以传入的参数。当你真正思考GPT-3、CodeX以及从它们过渡到Copilot的历程时，这不仅仅是模型的问题……

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Creating the model is one thing, but then figuring out how to use the model in terms of what parameters do you want to adjust for, what do you want to optimize for in terms of... A great example of this is performance, right? When you're in a code editor, you don't necessarily want to type, type, type and then have to wait one second, two seconds, three seconds to get a suggestion back when your entire goal is to stay in the flow. We would run experiments to see how many milliseconds are the right amount such that a developer doesn't feel like they're being interrupted by Copilot and a suggestion.
turns.zh: 创建模型是一回事，但如何在实际应用中调整参数、优化效果则是另一回事。以性能为例，当你在代码编辑器中工作时，肯定不想一遍又一遍地输入代码，然后还要等一秒、两秒、三秒才能得到建议——毕竟你的目标是保持流畅的工作状态。我们通过实验来确定，多少毫秒的延迟能让开发者感觉Copilot的建议没有打断他们的工作流程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the answer to that?
turns.zh: 答案是什么？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: It seems like right now it's around 200 milliseconds. Depending upon where you're in the world, your latency can go up or down a little bit from there. But it seems like the sweet spot is somewhere around 200 milliseconds.
turns.zh: 目前的数据是200毫秒左右。根据全球不同地区的网络延迟情况，这个数字可能会有上下浮动，但200毫秒左右似乎是一个理想的平衡点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good to know.
turns.zh: 这点很重要。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: We also experimented quite a bit. It's not just about the model, but it's also about what you feed the model. How do you prompt the model to return back a useful response? This kind of began a journey of experimentation for what we call prompt crafting.
turns.zh: 我们也进行了大量实验。关键不仅在于模型本身，还在于如何给模型提供有效的输入。如何引导模型返回有用的响应？这就开启了我们所谓的“提示工程”的探索之旅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going back to the way this started, it sounds like basically it was kind of this fortunate accident where OpenAI just did something that you didn't expect. And then somebody within this PhD group that you described is like, "Oh wow. Maybe we could do something really good with this." Is that kind of how it began?
turns.zh: 回顾整个过程，似乎这是一次幸运的意外。OpenAI做了一件出乎意料的事情，然后你提到的那个博士团队成员说"哇，太棒了，我们或许能用这个做些了不起的事。"对吧？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: That's fairly accurate. Yeah. I mean, we had a model that really was amazingly good, like a step level change in actual intelligence, right? And then marrying that up against a really good use case that actually changes developers' fundamental experience of the creation process, the creative process.
turns.zh: 这描述得很准确。是的。我们当时有一个模型，确实表现得极其出色，是实际智能水平的一次飞跃。然后，我们将它与一个真正优秀的用例相结合，这个用例彻底改变了开发者对创作过程、创新过程的基本体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was there kind of a point at which it was clear to you or leadership in general like, we should double down on this thing and go big? Or this smaller team was working on this idea and then you're like, "Oh wow, this is going to work?" Or is it always like, "We will bet on this thing, this is such a big and great idea. We're going to invest resources for sure from the beginning?"
turns.zh: 有没有一个转折点，让你或领导层意识到应该全力以赴、放手一搏？还是说这个小团队一直在推进这个想法，然后你突然意识到"哇，这真的能行"？还是说从一开始你们就坚信"我们要押注这个想法，这是一个宏大而伟大的创意，从一开始我们就必须投入资源"？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: The original team that was working on Copilot at GitHub was the team that we call GitHub Next. Essentially their job is to work on second and third horizon projects. What some folks might call moonshots, right? Things that we never really expect work in the next one or two years, but might three, five years down the line actually turn into something meaningful.
turns.zh: 最初在GitHub上开发Copilot的团队是我们称之为GitHub Next的团队。他们的主要职责是负责第二代和第三代的创新项目。有些人可能会称之为"登月计划"，对吧？那些我们预计未来一两年内无法实现，但可能在三五年后会真正产生重大影响的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a concrete definition of horizon two and three? Is it like number of years out like Amazon style?
turns.zh: 关于“第二和第三个视野”是否有具体定义？它是否像亚马逊那样设定为未来几年的时间跨度？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Not necessarily a concrete definition. For me, I usually ballpark it as first horizon is the next year, second horizon, the next three years, third horizon, the next five years. But we generally think of it more as a measure of ambiguity and confidence level more than calendar dates.
turns.zh: 这未必有固定的定义。对我来说，通常把第一视野设为未来一年，第二视野设为未来三年，第三视野设为未来五年。但我们更倾向于将其视为不确定性程度和信心水平的衡量标准，而非具体的日期。

Check them out at ModernTreasury.com. I'd love to spend a little bit more time on this. It's so interesting. Is this a Microsoft thing, just having these three horizons in a certain percentage of resources or bet on different horizons?
turns.zh: Modern Treasury的平台支持实时支付、自动对账、持续会计及合规解决方案，每月处理超30亿美元的对账业务。作为当今市场上最热门的金融科技初创公司之一，他们已从Benchmark、Altimeter、SVB Capital、Salesforce Ventures和Y Combinator等顶级机构融资。欢迎访问ModernTreasury.com。我想多聊聊这个话题。这太有趣了。这是微软的做法吗？是在一定比例的资源上设置这三个视野，还是在不同视野上下注？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: I would say it is not necessarily Microsoft thing, but is definitely at GitHub, how we have really contextualized it. Not to say that there aren't teams at Microsoft who might also use that methodology, but where we've been really maybe explicit or intentional about it is at GitHub where we've actually ring-fenced a team to think about that horizon two and horizon three work and kept them separate from EPD. EPD here being engineering, product, and design, the folks who are working on building productized operational products that we bring to market and we either give away or monetize in some way.
turns.zh: 我认为这不一定是微软的做法，但在GitHub，我们确实对此进行了深入实践。并非所有微软团队都使用这种方法，但在GitHub，我们确实特别设立了一个团队来专注于视野二和视野三的工作，并将其与EPD（工程、产品和设计）团队分开。EPD团队负责开发可商业化的产品，并通过免费或变现的方式推向市场。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting. There's a lot of companies that have these sorts of R&D groups, new product experience team at Facebook and Google has one. I'm not sure how many successes have come out of these teams. From what I've seen, and I'm curious, what have you... And clearly you had a huge success as far as I can tell so far. Is there anything you've learned about how to do this, where you invest in these big moonshots within a larger company?
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。许多公司都有这样的研发团队，比如Facebook和谷歌的NPE团队。我不确定这些团队取得了多少成功。就我所见，我很好奇，你们是如何在大公司内部投资这些大胆的创新项目的？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: I mean, I think the first step is to invest in it. The first step is really hire really smart people, attract smart people, and give them the opportunity to be creative. Don't expect anything out of them that is going to turn into a money maker or something that is going to be beholden to fundamentals around security, privacy, uptime, accessibility, all that groovy kind of stuff upfront. They need space to create and experiment.
turns.zh: 我认为第一步是投入资源。第一步就是招聘真正聪明的人，吸引优秀人才，并给予他们创造的空间。不要期望他们一开始就能创造出赚钱的项目，也不要要求他们必须遵守安全、隐私、正常运行时间、可访问性等基本准则。这些团队需要有自由发挥的空间去创新和试验。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: And also, when you do get to a place where that team has an idea that is clearly connected to a representative set of customers who have a genuine problem and there is signal with at least medium confidence that this solution, whatever it is, solves it in a novel way, that's the time to start thinking about, okay, let's actually put a little bit of... I'm going to call this market testing. It's nothing so formal as market testing. It's really just like, let's start to actually bring prototypes of this in front of more and more customers to kind of test it out and see, hey, is this actually solving a problem for you? Is this something that you would use? This is where the transition between Next and EPD at GitHub really started.
turns.zh: 另外，当你发现团队提出的方案能清晰对应一群有真实需求的客户，并且有至少中等置信度的信号表明，无论解决方案如何创新，都能切实解决问题时，这就是时候开始考虑：好吧，让我们投入一点精力……我把这称为市场测试。虽然不算正式的市场测试，但本质上就是让越来越多的客户试用产品原型，观察他们是否能解决问题，感知他们的真实需求。这正是GitHub Next与EPD团队合作的转折点。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: This is actually where my role in the product cycle kind of really started to increase. I had kind of been in tight connection and been monitoring the work and kind of consulting a little bit with the Next team prior to that. But it was that moment when we identified that, okay, this is actually something real. Customers are saying, developers are saying, "This is magical. This does something extraordinary that I could not do on my own," that we started to think about, okay, how do we transition this over? From there, we're really just like, okay, we think we've got a hit here. We think we've got something that we can actually bring to developers.
turns.zh: 实际上，我的角色在产品周期中也随之提升。在此之前，我一直与Next团队保持密切联系，监督进展并提供咨询。但正是当我们确认方案切实可行——客户和开发者纷纷惊呼“太神奇了！这真是我自己无法实现的奇迹”——时，我们开始思考如何将其推广。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: We made an intentional decision to take some of the researchers who were in the Next team and for a finite period of time, move them over to create a new EPD squad. We want them to be researchers, but we need to do knowledge transfer and we needed to actually provide the seed for a team that could eventually operationalize and productize. And that kind of began the technical preview where we started to invite tens of thousands, then hundreds of thousands to the technical preview. In that technical preview, we started to see crazy mind-blown emoji tweets and threads on Hacker News about people getting really, really excited about it.
turns.zh: 我们特意将Next团队的研究人员抽调出来，组成EPD小组。在有限的时间内，他们以研究者的身份参与其中，但需要进行知识传递，为最终能够实现产品化和商业化的团队奠定基础。随之而来的是技术预览阶段，我们先邀请数万名用户参与，后来又扩展至数十万人。期间，我们看到Hacker News上用户们兴奋不已，纷纷发布惊喜表情和讨论帖。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: That's how we knew it was time to start scaling and it was time to really start thinking about how do we do hiring so that we can build in some insulation around these researchers so that they can eventually go back to GitHub Next to do what they do best, which is be innovative and creative and think about the next moonshot. That process, that took... Well, we're actually still kind of at the tail end of it now. Here we are, like I said, roughly a year and a half after the initial creation of the product, having gone through technical preview, have achieved general availability. We've now hired in a team around them.
turns.zh: 这让我们意识到是时候扩大规模，思考如何招募人才，为这些研究人员创造缓冲区，让他们能回归GitHub Next，专注创新和下一个突破性项目。目前这个进程仍在推进。正如我所说，产品诞生一年半后，我们完成了技术预览，正式上线，并组建了专门团队。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: The researchers actually as early as last month have started to gradually move back over to GitHub Next. An EPD squad, multiple EPD squads actually are now taking the product forward and starting to respond to customer feedback to think about, okay, how do we now as a product team, carry this roadmap forward from an idea that originated in GitHub Next?
turns.zh: 早在上个月，研究人员就开始陆续回归GitHub Next。多个EPD团队正接力推进产品，结合客户反馈，思考如何作为产品团队，将这份诞生于GitHub Next的愿景延续下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that insight of bringing the people along and not just kind of like, cool, we'll take it from here. If you were to build a team like this again somewhere to this kind of R&D horizon three or two teams, is there anything else you would do differently, any lessons you take away from this experience for maybe founders or PMs working at larger companies that are like, "Hey, we should have something like this?" Is there anything else that you find is important for making something like this successful?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏那种让团队成员全程参与其中的理念，而不是简单地说"好的，接下来我们接手吧"。如果你要在某个地方再组建一个类似的研发团队——无论是三支还是两支——有没有什么可以改进的地方？有没有什么经验教训可以传授给那些在大公司工作的创始人或产品经理，让他们觉得"嘿，我们也应该搞个这样的团队"？还有什么因素对成功打造这样的团队至关重要？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: The criteria for moving researchers back into their R&D team, whatever that happens to be for your organization, that can't be based on a calendar. It needs to be based on a replacement in seat, who's actually doing the job and has picked up all of the skills necessary, and only then can the researcher move back. Make sure that you've got continuity of expertise and sets and domain familiarity before you move over. I feel like we've managed that pretty well today. As well, it's critical that the team who is taking over from the R&D shop feels like they have control over their own future. You can't really delegate roadmap to an R&D team.
turns.zh: 无论在你所在的组织中如何安排研发团队成员的回归，都不能基于日历安排。必须基于职位空缺情况，即谁真正胜任了这份工作，掌握了所有必要技能之后，研发团队成员才能回归。在回归之前，要确保专业知识和技能的延续性，以及对领域的熟悉度。我觉得我们今天在这方面做得不错。同样，至关重要的是，接管研发团队的团队要觉得自己能掌控自己的未来。不能把路线图完全外包给研发团队。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: The team who's responsible for maintaining the product, for building the product, who has the closest feedback loop with the end customer, they're the ones who really need to own and feel like they control the roadmap. Making sure that you're not outsourcing innovation exclusively to an R&D team, but that is happening within the product team as they take ownership over the idea and over the use case in the customer. Last I would say here is really that engineering fundamentals in a lot of ways are the contracts that differentiate an R&D team from an operational product team.
turns.zh: 负责维护产品、构建产品、与终端客户有最紧密反馈循环的团队，才是真正需要拥有并掌控路线图的团队。确保你不是把创新完全外包给研发团队，而是让产品团队在接手想法和客户用例时就开始掌控创新。最后我想说的是，工程基础知识在很多方面是区分研发团队和运营型产品团队的契约。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Bringing that fundamentals process into it is going to feel candidly a little bit unnatural to the researchers. That takes therefore a little bit of cultural change management for everyone to just adapt their way of working and understand that we're graduating from an experiment and a research project to an operational product, and often because those researchers are... They're the first wave that come over. They're the seed of the project. It's going to feel a little bit unnatural to them and they probably won't have all the right skillsets in order to make that transition.
turns.zh: 把这些基础流程引入研发团队，对研究人员来说坦白说会有点不自然。因此，这需要进行一定的文化变革管理，让每个人适应新的工作方式，理解我们正在从实验和研究项目过渡到运营型产品。通常，这些研究人员是首批加入的成员，是项目的种子。对他们来说，这会感觉有点不自然，而且他们可能不具备完成这种过渡所需的全部技能。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Making sure that you've got a good mix of engineers who are comfortable maintaining a service, as well as engineers and researchers who are really thinking about, what is the idea that we've created, what is the new thing that we've brought to market, and can bring that vision to it.
turns.zh: 确保团队中有既能胜任维护服务的工程师，也有真正思考我们创造了什么理念、带来了什么新事物的工程师和研究人员，并能为此注入愿景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I can totally see the challenge that comes from... This was my thing. I've been working on this. What are you guys doing to this project? Where is this going? I'm not sure I'm feeling... And then there's all these new asks that are coming at you like, oh my God, this was so much fun and now I have to scale this freaking thing.
turns.zh: 是的，我完全能理解这种挑战……这曾是我的专长。我一直致力于此。你们对这个项目做了什么？它要走向何方？我不确定自己是否能适应……然后又有各种新的要求向你涌来——天哪，这曾经如此有趣，现在却要把这破玩意儿规模化。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: I mean, this is the best problem in the world to have. Talk about kind of customer ask, for Copilot in particular, the amount of chatter, the amount of customer feedback that was coming in especially for us with AI, I mean, the world is still figuring out AI, candidly. I mean, we're getting a lot better at it, especially in the last couple of years with things like Dolly and Copilot. But it brings with it not only engineering challenges, but also, frankly, ethical challenges and legal challenges, like making sense of what our expectations are of AI. If AI produces something that is offensive, who's at fault?
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这是世界上最理想的难题了。谈到Copilot的用户反馈，尤其是涉及人工智能的部分，用户的反馈量实在惊人。说实话，全球都在探索人工智能的边界。我们在过去几年里确实进步显著，比如Dolly和Copilot等技术。但随之而来的不仅是工程挑战，还有伦理和法律难题——比如如何界定我们对人工智能的期望？如果AI产出带有攻击性的内容，谁该为此负责？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Our stance on it, what we ended up coming to is actually the framing of Copilot as an AI pair programmer I think is a useful one. Pair programmer, I suspect most of your listeners will know, but pair programmer is usually two developers sitting side by side working on a problem together. One's at the keyboard and the other one's kind of helping them talk through it, talk through the ideas and make corrections, that kind of thing. Well, if Copilot is your AI pair programmer and they're whispering crazy stuff into your ear and they're bringing politics into it or gender identity into it or, I don't know, whatever other...
turns.zh: 我们最终达成的共识是，将Copilot定义为"人工智能编程搭档"这个概念非常有用。编程搭档，相信听众大多熟悉这个概念——通常是指两位开发者并排协作解决问题。一个负责敲代码，另一个则提供思路指导、修正错误等支持。但如果Copilot充当你的AI搭档，却在你耳边乱喷政治言论、攻击性别认同等等敏感内容，你肯定无法专心工作吧？这无疑会严重分散注意力。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: They're spouting off slang and slander and all that kind of stuff. You're probably not going to be able to focus on your work, right? It's going to be really distracting. Really coming down to some principles about what is the use case we're trying to solve, what is appropriate, I put this in scare quotes, behavior of the AI bot sitting side by side with you, helped us create some principles or some guidelines for the developer experience that we wanted to create.
turns.zh: 归根结底，我们需要明确Copilot的使用场景，以及与开发者交互时的恰当行为规范。为此，我们制定了一系列开发者体验指南。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I love that. Just kind of creating a persona of the thing to help you inform how the behavior of the thing should work. How do you work through these challenges? Is it discussions with you and the legal team? I don't know, these ethical things are really tricky, I imagine. How do you approach them like that as a product team?
turns.zh: 哦，我太喜欢这个思路了。通过构建AI的虚拟人格，指导其行为规范。你们是如何克服这些挑战的？是与法律团队的反复讨论吗？这些伦理问题确实棘手，我能想象。作为产品团队，你们是如何应对的？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: It is conversations with a very, very wide cast of characters. This product in particular, I probably spent more time with legal than any other products that I've ever kind of been responsible for. All wonderful creative people. But it's not just legal. It is also privacy and security champions. It is, frankly, developers, like the people who are using it, listening to them. Hey, what works here? What doesn't work for you here? Why is this offensive? Why is it not offensive? We'll continue on the example of the crazy pair programmer whispering crazy things into our year. When we first started out, we didn't really have any filter on Copilot whatsoever the very, very, very early days.
turns.zh: 这需要与各界人士广泛沟通。就这个产品而言，我与法律团队的沟通时间比我负责过的其他产品都要多。都是才华横溢的创意人才。但不止于法律层面，还涉及隐私与安全专家，以及开发者群体——毕竟他们才是直接用户。我们倾听他们的反馈：哪些功能好用？哪些体验糟糕？为何某些内容会引发不适？为何有些又无伤大雅？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: And then eventually we're like, okay, it needs to be slightly more controlled experience. We need to edit out some of the most egregious stuff. We introduced a simple block list of words, and these block lists are always fraught with peril, like which words are okay, which words are not okay. All of a sudden, we become editors of language and that's kind of a scary place to be. I'm not comfortable with it at least. But at a certain level, it has to be done, because otherwise you're going to create a bad developer experience.
turns.zh: 以疯狂编程搭档乱喷奇谈怪论为例。早期我们对Copilot完全没有过滤机制。后来，我们逐渐意识到需要控制内容输出。首先建立了关键词黑名单，但这类过滤机制总伴随着伦理风险——哪些词该屏蔽，哪些词又可以保留？突然间，我们成了语言的编辑者，这实在令人不安。至少我个人对此心存顾虑。但为了提供优质的开发者体验，某些程度的管控是必要的。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Often we would get feedback from developers of like, "Hey, this particular word was blocked. That it was blocked either was offensive to me or prevented me from being able to get good value out of the product."
turns.zh: 通常，我们会收到开发者反馈，比如：“嘿，这个特定的词被屏蔽了。被屏蔽的原因要么是冒犯了我的感觉，要么是让我无法充分利用这款产品。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Always kind of dancing the dance of editorial content. We're actually at a place now where we're able to partner with the Azure Department of a Responsible AI, and they've created some really extraordinary models that help detect I'll call it sentiment for lack of a better word, but basically when there is something that is patently offensive. Because there are some words that in some contexts may be offensive and in some context may be totally reasonable, especially when you get into software for medical kind of scenarios, right?
turns.zh: 在处理编辑内容方面，我们总是如履薄冰。现在我们与微软Azure的负责任人工智能部门合作，他们开发了一些非常出色的模型，能够检测到所谓的"情感"——虽然有些词在某些语境下可能具有冒犯性，但在某些情况下又完全合理，尤其是在医疗场景的软件开发中。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Being able to start to shift a little bit to focus or to rely on AI models that can also do a better job than we could with crude or simple block lists is maybe another proof point both of how AI as a solution for common development problems is getting way better at solving more parts of our stack or filling in for more parts of our stack. At least in our case, we were pretty fortunate to be able to deliver on or depend on a parent company's contributions to solve a real acute problem that GitHub probably could not have solved on our own.
turns.zh: 能够逐渐转向依赖人工智能模型，而不是依赖粗糙的黑名单来处理这些问题，这或许再次证明了人工智能作为解决常见开发难题的方案，正在越来越好地覆盖我们技术栈的更多领域，或填补更多空白。至少对我们来说，能依赖母公司的贡献来解决GitHub自身可能无法独立解决的尖锐问题，我们感到非常幸运。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I never thought that Copilot would be... That you would have to worry about it saying things that are crazy. That is wild that you guys have to deal with that. Wasn't it Microsoft that had that bot that turned really negative and eventually shut down?
turns.zh: 我从没想过Copilot会……还得担心它说出一些疯狂的话。你们居然要处理这种情况，这也太疯狂了。不就是微软那个机器人变得很负面，最后被关闭了吗？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: It was.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's experience there.
turns.zh: 这方面我们有经验。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: What was its name? Talia or something like that?
turns.zh: 它叫什么名字？塔莉亚之类的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something like that.
turns.zh: 差不多吧。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Yeah, something like that. We don't want another one of those incidences.
turns.zh: 对，大概是这样。我们可不想再出现那种情况了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. What this makes me think about is your team is at the forefront of AI in this applied way. I'm curious what your thinking is on just where this goes for developers especially. I saw a stat that maybe 40% of people's code is now written by Copilot. I don't know if that's right. But is the vision in the future becomes something like 90? Where do you see this all going?
turns.zh: 哇。这让我想到，你们团队在应用人工智能方面走在前沿。我很好奇你们对开发者们尤其有什么看法。我看到一项统计数据，说现在40%的人的代码是由Copilot编写的。不知道这数据是否准确。但未来会不会达到90%？你们觉得这一切会发展到什么地步？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Just to put a fine point on that stat, it is 40% is specifically for Python developers. Candidly, it varies depending upon the language. Because as you might imagine, some languages have better representation in the public domain than others. And usually both the volume and the diversity of training data correlates with the quality of suggestions, which is then represented by either the number of lines written or the acceptance rate or any one of a number of other metrics.
turns.zh: 具体来说，这个40%是针对Python开发者的。说实话，这个比例因语言而异。因为你可以想象，有些语言在公共领域的代表性比其他语言更强。通常，训练数据的数量和多样性与建议的质量相关，而建议的质量又体现在编写的代码行数、接受率或其他一些指标上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Thanks for clarifying.
turns.zh: 太棒了。感谢你的解释。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Yeah, totally. We see it range anywhere from the upper twenties to the forties across all the different languages.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。我们看到不同语言的范围从20%多到40%不等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to throw this out there, as a not great engineer, I used to be an engineer for about 10 years, I welcome our AI Overlords writing all my code. I'm excited for this to do more and more. And yes, I'm curious where you think this goes.
turns.zh: 先说一句，作为一个不算出色的工程师，我曾当了约10年的工程师。我欢迎我们的AI霸主们来写我所有的代码。我很期待这项技术能不断发展壮大。是的，我很好奇你们认为它会走向何方。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: It does. It enables even mediocre developers like myself to be able to do some pretty amazing things. But where's it going? First, I think, I hope it's obvious to most developers that AI is going to infuse pretty much our entire development stack in the not so distant future. Copilot is really just the very tip of the sphere for a lot of innovations and better managing maybe our build queues or helping to... Here's a great one. I don't know about you, but often the comments that I get with commit messages and PRs aren't super great. It puts a lot of effort onto the code reviewer to go figure out what the developer was actually trying to do.
turns.zh: 确实如此。它让像我这样平庸的开发者也能做一些相当惊人的事情。但它会走向何方呢？首先，我认为——或者说我希望——大多数开发者都能明显感受到，AI将在不久的将来渗透到我们整个开发栈中。Copilot只是众多创新和优化工作的冰山一角，比如更好地管理构建队列或帮助……这里有个很棒的例子。我不知道你们怎么想，但我经常收到commit消息和PR评论，这些评论质量往往不高。这就需要代码审查者花费大量精力去理解开发者的真正意图。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: What if AI could summarize all of your changes with your full request and you just have to, as the contributing developer, just review it to make sure it's accurate, send it on its way, and you don't have to put in extra effort for that. There are lots and lots of different opportunities for AI to essentially be able to take some of the drudgery out of our work so that we can focus on creative acts. What I hear from developers and what I experience myself is that Copilot kind of forces me to think a little bit more about what are the design patterns I'm trying to create?
turns.zh: 如果AI能根据你的完整请求总结所有变更，而作为贡献开发者，你只需检查其准确性并提交即可，那不是很棒吗？AI还有无数的机会能消除我们工作中的繁琐任务，让我们专注于创造性工作。从开发者那里听到的，也是我自己的体验，Copilot迫使我更多地思考我想要创建的设计模式是什么？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: What is the end user experience or the outcomes that I'm trying to drive with my code, and that I can rely on Copilot to scaffold out a lot of that so that I can focus on more creative work? That is really what I hope for our industry five, 10 years from now, is that not only will we be inviting more developers or more people to become developers by essentially providing a layer of abstraction a little bit, or at least a little bit of a hand in development, but that also the really experienced developers are focusing on much larger problems and focusing on outcomes and creativity rather than really low level difficult rote memorization of things like syntax or ordering of parameters and the like.
turns.zh: 最终用户体验或我希望通过代码实现的结果是什么？我可以依赖Copilot搭建大部分框架，这样我就能专注于更有创意的工作。这正是我对未来五年、十年行业发展的期待：我们不仅要通过提供一定的抽象层或开发辅助，吸引更多人成为开发者，还要让真正经验丰富的开发者专注于更宏大的问题和成果，而非纠结于语法、参数顺序之类的低级难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. If nothing else, that'll keep people from just having a tab of Stack Overflow, copy and pasting every function that they're trying to figure out.
turns.zh: 太好了。如果没有别的，这至少能让人们不再在Stack Overflow上开着标签，复制粘贴他们试图理解的每个函数了。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: I want Stack Overflow to stay in business, but I would mind a little bit less contact switching myself.
turns.zh: 我希望Stack Overflow能继续运营下去，但我不太希望自己频繁切换联系方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the experience of scaling this thing, what would you say has been the biggest challenge either technologically or even operationally just kind of scaling it to a real product that people are paying for?
turns.zh: 在扩展这项技术的过程中，技术上或运营上最大的挑战是什么？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: There's a few dimensions of that. One is a problem that's very much of our time in the world, namely that supply chains have been disrupted dramatically over the course of the last few years. It turns out that Copilot for both training and operating the models requires some very rare and unique GPUs that there's not a lot of global supply of. Part of it is just like, can we get enough hardware in order to run these things? We've actually earmarked quite a bit of capacity, and we are greedy, greedy, greedy for more capacity globally. As soon as we can produce those chips and get them in data centers, we do it.
turns.zh: 这涉及几个层面的问题。其中之一是我们这个时代普遍面临的挑战——供应链在过去几年里遭遇了严重的断供。事实上，训练和运行Copilot模型所需的GPU极为稀缺，全球供应量严重不足。核心问题在于，我们能否获取足够的硬件来支持模型运行？为此，我们已投入大量资源，并正持续加大全球硬件产能，一旦芯片制造完成并投入数据中心，我们就会立即部署。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: That's been one kind of unique challenge. I would also say here that operationally, another challenge has been, how do we create a model that the community really feels like ownership over, right? The dialogue that's had to happen as we brought an AI tool to market, especially one that is trained on public code, has required a lot of dialogue between us and our community. Every good product manager should be spending as much of their time as possible with their customers, with their potential customers.
turns.zh: 这是首个独特挑战。另一方面，运营层面也面临挑战——如何让社区真正接纳并认同Copilot模型？将AI工具推向市场，尤其是基于公开代码训练的模型，需要与社区展开深度对话。优秀的产品经理应当尽可能多地与客户及潜在客户沟通。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Copilot, in particular, has been a more complicated kind of rollout because we as an industry, as a society are still figuring out how to make sense of it. The amount of give and take between developers and us as a product team has really required us to scale up more of the product team than it has the engineering team.
turns.zh: Copilot的推广尤为复杂，因为整个行业乃至社会仍在探索如何正确理解这项技术。开发者与产品团队之间的反复磨合，促使我们在产品团队而非工程团队上投入了更多资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. And why is that?
turns.zh: 有意思。原因何在？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: It's a couple of different reasons. I mean, one, like I said, we are trained on public code. Not all of the community is really sure like, when is it okay to train a model on public code? When is it not okay to train a model on public code? Is Copilot producing secure suggestions? Is Copilot producing bug buggy suggestions? There's a lot of doubt. There's a lot of very healthy skepticism. Actually I mean that genuinely. I want people to be skeptical of Copilot. We owe it to ourselves as a community to be skeptical of any AI.
turns.zh: 有多重原因。首先，Copilot基于公开代码训练。并非所有开发者都清楚：何时可以使用公开代码训练模型？何时又不宜如此？Copilot生成的建议是否安全？是否存在漏洞？这些疑虑完全合理。我们真心希望人们对Copilot保持质疑——作为社区成员，我们有责任对任何AI技术保持警惕。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Because just like there's great potential for benefit, there's also great potential for harm. People keeping us accountable like, how are you preventing things like model poisoning? Is there going to be a new attack vector that we just haven't really thought of yet around AI that might produce negative consequences? We think that we've done a really good and responsible job of that by making sure that first, we are very clear that Copilot is not a replacement for a developer. It will never be.
turns.zh: 正如技术可能带来巨大益处，也可能引发严重危害。人们时刻监督我们：如何防止模型中毒？是否会出现我们尚未预见的AI攻击载体？为此，我们通过以下措施尽到责任：首先明确Copilot并非开发者的替代品，永远不会取代开发者。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: We do not want Copilot auto generating code where a thinking, reasoning, breathing human being is not on the other side of that keyboard making recent decisions. We do not want Copilot to replace any other part of the stack, whether it is static analysis tools or your unit tests or whatever kind of measures you're putting in today to make sure that your humans produce good quality code. We want you to keep all of those same systems in place to make sure that humans who are leveraging tools like Copilot continue to produce that good quality code.
turns.zh: 我们绝不允许Copilot自动生成代码，除非有人坐在键盘前实时决策。我们不希望Copilot取代任何其他环节——无论是静态分析工具、单元测试，还是现有确保开发者产出高质量代码的机制。我们要求用户继续使用现有系统，确保借助Copilot等工具的开发者始终能产出高质量代码。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: But there's a lot of at the same time anxiety of like, where is AI stack? Is AI eventually going to be... This is back to your question about where will we be five, 10 years from now. Will it be writing 90% of the code? We don't want Copilot to be that... We don't want it to replace anything. We want it to augment. The idea here is really that AI is an enabler for developers to focus on the creative work, to stay in the flow, to be able to move faster. Working through those anxieties, working through that healthy skepticism takes conversation. It takes dialogue. And that takes us on the product side having that guided conversation with the community.
turns.zh: 与此同时，人们也深感焦虑，比如人工智能的发展进程如何？人工智能最终会取代人类吗？这又回到了你提出的五年、十年后我们将处于何种境地的问题。届时会编写90%的代码吗？我们不希望Copilot成为那样……我们不希望它取代任何东西，而是要增强人类的能力。这里的核心理念是，人工智能应当成为开发者的助力，帮助他们专注于创造性工作，保持工作流畅，加快开发进度。克服这些焦虑，化解这种健康的怀疑，需要对话与交流。这就要求我们在产品层面与社区开展有引导性的对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like it connects back to your education back in the day, philosophy and literature. How convenient is that?
turns.zh: 这似乎与你早年的教育背景——哲学和文学——息息相关。真是太巧了！

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: It often feels very connect... I mean, certainly the education side of things taught me that the importance of dialogue, the importance of skepticism is valuable in so much more than esoteric armchair ponderings. It's actually applicable to the real world.
turns.zh: 这种关联感确实很强烈……当然，教育经历让我深刻认识到，对话和怀疑精神的价值远不止于深奥的纸上谈兵，它们在现实世界中同样适用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe a final question before we get to our very exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 在我们即将进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后再问一个问题。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Woo!
turns.zh: 哇！

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just looking back at this whole experience of, one, just building, incubating, launching this big bold bet within a big company, you can go in either direction, either just any lessons on just taking a bold bet versus incremental wins and how you think about investing in these two kind of categories, or just within a large company, a lesson of just how to build something like this, like a massive new product from just a seed of an idea to a large new business line potentially.
turns.zh: 回顾整个经历，首先是构建、孵化、推出这一大胆的创新项目。在大公司内部，如何选择是专注于大胆的押注还是渐进式胜利，如何看待这两种策略之间的投入差异？又或者如何从种子般的创意，逐步打造出全新的大型产品线？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: As both a product manager and a portfolio manager of multiple products, I'm responsible for multiple product lines at GitHub, the allocation of time, of focus, energy, and resources becomes a really challenging question. The answer to which isn't always the same, depending upon the time, world circumstances, organizational circumstances, technology circumstances. As a general rule, as a general principle, I certainly try to make sure that we're always reserving some capacity for bold, audacious experimental research projects. You can think of those really uncertain bets as being five to 10% of the team's capacity. About 25, maybe 30% of the team's capacity should generally be on just operations.
turns.zh: 作为产品经理和多个产品的投资组合经理，我在GitHub负责多个产品线。如何分配时间、精力和资源，成为一个极具挑战性的问题。答案因时而异，受制于市场环境、组织架构和技术条件。总体而言，我始终确保为大胆的实验性研究项目保留一定的空间。可以将这些高风险、高不确定性的项目视为团队产能的5%至10%。约25%至30%的团队产能应专注于现有产品的运营优化。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: How do we keep our in-market products meeting customer expectations? And then the remainder of it, what is that, about 60% or so, is really on incremental progress for our end market products. How do we make iterative improvements and continue to actually realize payoff for the larger bets that we made one, two, three, four years back? And from a rough distribution, that's generally how I run my larger teams. That works when you have larger teams though. At startups, where we were pretty much only a big bet, obviously your percentages get very different and it becomes a matter of you're all in for that one proverbial lottery ticket.
turns.zh: 如何确保在市场产品满足客户期望的同时，将剩余资源投入到增量改进中？大约60%的精力应专注于现有产品的迭代优化，如何为一两年前做出的重大决策持续创造价值？从大团队的经验来看，这样的分配模式行之有效。但在初创公司，团队往往只有一个高风险的赌注，投入比例则完全不同，所有人都押注在那张传说中的彩票上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Thanks for sharing that. I was going to ask you the percentages that you recommend. Thank you for getting to that. With that, we've gotten to our very exciting lightning round. I'm just going to ask you five questions briefly and just whatever comes to mind, whatever answer you have. Let's do it. Sound good? Okay. What are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 太棒了。谢谢你分享这些。我本来想问问你推荐的百分比是多少。谢谢你提到这一点。接下来是我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。我会快速问你五个问题，想到什么就说什么，想到什么回答什么。准备好了吗？好的。你最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Oh, good question. One of them is a book on user experience called Make It So. It's a reference back to Star Trek, and the idea here is essentially that user experiences that are presented to us in sci-fi often make their way into our everyday products and tools 20, 30 years down the line. It is a great eye-opening, illuminating and just really fun book. That's one. And then completely different take, I'll go outside of tech and I'll just do entertainment value. There's a David Foster Wallace book called Brief Interviews with Hideous Men that I love. It's a collection of short stories.
turns.zh: 哦，这个问题问得好。第一本是关于用户体验的书，叫《Make It So》。这本书引用了《星际迷航》里的台词，核心观点是科幻作品中呈现的用户体验，往往会在20、30年后融入我们的日常产品和工具。这本书极具启发性，既有趣又发人深省。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: And essentially what it is, is it is if you're watching a movie and the villain gets their opportunity to have their big speech, which kind of explains why they are who they are, it makes them maybe a little bit vulnerable in that moment, it's that speech 10 times over for different hideous people, terrible, terrible people. Interesting read. I recommend it.
turns.zh: 再说个完全不同的推荐，我要跳出科技领域，推荐娱乐类书籍。大卫·福斯特·华莱士的《与可怕男人的简短访谈》这本书我很喜欢，是短篇小说集。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. It reminds me of this book that is the interior design of dictators and they show you their homes of Saddam Hussein, Hitler, and all these guys.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这本书。它让我想起另一本关于独裁者住宅的书，展示了萨达姆·侯赛因、希特勒等人的住所。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Dude! Oh my gosh, that's awesome. I got to find that one. You'll have to send it to me.
turns.zh: 天哪！太棒了。我得去找找看。你能发给我吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I found one at an old bookstore, like used bookstore. I don't know if they're around anymore, but I'll find it. Second question. What's a favorite other podcast that you like to listen to or recommend if there's any?
turns.zh: 我在一家旧书店找到了。不知道现在还有没有这种书店，但我会找到的。第二个问题。你有没有喜欢的播客推荐？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Oh god, there's so many. I consume hundreds of hours of podcasts every month. It is crazy. I can choose many. I'll give you just one. The Memory Palace with Nate DiMeo is an excellent storytelling podcast. He does about 20 minute vignettes, usually selected from kind of American history. He also was the artist in residence at one of the museums in Washington, DC. And if you're ever at I think it's the American History Museum or something like that, if you're ever there, you can go to different rooms in the museum and he'll tell you stories about the objects or the rooms that you see there. It's a magical experience recommended to anyone.
turns.zh: 天哪，太多了。我每个月听上百小时的播客，简直疯狂。我可以选一个。推荐《记忆宫殿》，这个播客由内特·迪梅奥主持，讲述精彩故事。每集约20分钟，内容多选自美国历史。他还曾在华盛顿特区某博物馆担任驻场艺术家。如果你去过美国历史博物馆之类的地方，可以参观不同展厅，他会讲述展品或房间背后的故事。这绝对是种神奇体验，强烈推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow! I love those. What's a recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 哇！我喜欢这类作品。最近有没有你特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: I don't know if this counts as recent, but it's one that I watched recently, which was Arrival. Yeah, that counts. Arrival. Movie ostensibly about aliens, but is really about language and memory. I found that really, really compelling.
turns.zh: 不确定算不算新片，但我最近看了《降临》。这部电影表面上讲外星人，实质探讨语言和记忆。我觉得非常引人入胜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you read Ted Chiang books and short stories?
turns.zh: 你读过泰德·张的书和短篇小说吗？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: I have not. I have not.
turns.zh: 没读过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow! Oh, you would love it. Arrival is from one of his story, I believe, is one of his stories and there's a whole book of many more short stories by the same guy. They're amazing.
turns.zh: 天哪！你肯定会喜欢的。《降临》就源自他的一篇短篇小说集，同名作者还有更多短篇小说集，都很棒。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Brilliant. I've got my weekend cut out for me then.
turns.zh: 太棒了。看来我的周末安排满满当当了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There you go. Just leave work and get to reading. What's a favorite interview question that you like to ask in interviews?
turns.zh: 好吧，那你下班后就专心阅读吧。你最喜欢在面试中问哪个问题？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: Let's see here. I'll give you a fun one more than it is a challenging one. This is kind of my icebreaker interview question, particularly for more early to mid career product managers. I ask them to teach me something new in one minute. Usually I'll pull up my phone and I'll start the timer. I'll give them a second to think about it and start the timer. They're graded on three different criteria. One is completeness. Did they actually finish the lesson inside of one minute? Two is complexity. It's one thing if you teach me how to, I don't know, pat my head and rub my stomach at the same time.
turns.zh: 让我想想。我会选一个比较有趣而非难答的问题。这算是我常用的破冰提问，尤其适合处于职业生涯早期至中期的产品经理。我会让他们用一分钟时间教我新东西。通常我会拿出手机，启动计时器。给他们一秒钟思考，然后再启动计时器。评分标准有三个：一是完成度。他们能否在一分钟内完成教学内容？二是复杂度。比如教我同时拍拍头、揉揉肚子这种简单动作，显然比不上讲解18世纪宗教思潮的复杂内容。三是清晰度。关键在于我是否真正理解了，是否学到了东西，他们是否把知识完整传达出来了。

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: It's another thing if you teach me something about 18th century ardent connection to religious trends at the time. And then last is really clarity. Oh yeah, clarity is the last one. Clarity is like, do I actually understand? Did I learn something by the end of the lesson? Did they convey the idea fully and wholly?
turns.zh: 你最感兴趣的回答是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have to ask, what's the most interesting thing somebody has taught in this question?
turns.zh: 我得问问，最有趣的回答是什么？

turns.speaker: Ryan J. Salva
turns.en: My go-to kind of throwaway answer there about did they teach me something about 18th century art and its connection to religious trends at the time, someone taught me that. It was astounding. It was actually a university candidate, so someone who was still in university, and she was from Vanderbilt University.
